blogs.title: Intrinsic Acts vs. Propensity: The Eighth Circuit's Expansive View of 'Continuous Possession' in Felon-in-Possession Cases
blogs.description: This post analyzes the court's treatment of Federal Rule of Evidence 404(b) regarding the admission of prior sightings of the firearm. It examines the Eighth Circuit's reliance on *United States v. Battle* to classify evidence of the defendant holding the gun on previous occasions as 'intrinsic' rather than impermissible character evidence. The analysis will explore the tension between proving 'continuous possession'—an element of the crime—and the risk of inviting jurors to convict based on a defendant's general propensity for violence, particularly given the horrific nature of the underlying domestic assault.

blogs.title: The Limits of Appellate Advocacy: Waiver, Forfeiture, and the Court's Rebuke of 'Expanded' Issues
blogs.description: Focusing on Section II(E), this post dissects the appellate panel's sharp criticism of the government for raising an unpreserved argument regarding cross-examination limits, noting the court's remark that it does 'not appreciate appellees who unnecessarily expand the issues on appeal.' Despite this rebuke, the court proceeded to address the merits under plain error review. The article will discuss what this signals about the Eighth Circuit's approach to waiver versus forfeiture in criminal appeals and how strictly practitioners must adhere to preservation rules when facing a bench willing to sua sponte address unpreserved claims if the outcome is clear.

blogs.title: Double Counting or Statutory Mandate? Navigating the Intersection of ACCA Mandatory Minimums and USSG § 2K2.1 Enhancements
blogs.description: This post addresses the sentencing controversy where the defendant argued that applying a four-level enhancement for possessing a firearm 'in connection with another felony' (§ 2K2.1(b)(6)(B)) resulted in a sentence conflicting with 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a)'s 'sufficient but not greater than necessary' principle. The analysis will explain how the Guidelines' structure (specifically § 4B1.4) mandates applying whichever calculation yields a higher offense level, effectively layering sentencing enhancements atop Armed Career Criminal Act (ACCA) findings. It will evaluate whether the Eighth Circuit's affirmation suggests a rigid adherence to guideline mechanics over individualized proportionality arguments in cases involving violent felons.
